https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-bur.text: NEW YORK — Before Andy Burnham’s meeting with Donald Trump, a senior U.K. government figure noted wryly that they were looking out for one thing — whether the U.S. president would claim that Burnham was better than the last guy. After nearly an hour together in a cramped, low-ceilinged room in the United Nations basement, Trump did exactly that. The president said U.K.-U.S. relations were “more up now than they were with your last prime minister.” Moments later he put the boot into Keir Starmer again, claiming the ex-PM’s tough rhetoric on Russia had been “too tough.” Advertisement Advertisement That final comment will please Starmer, who welcomed Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Britain after Trump berated him in the Oval Office. But it also shows how far his relationship with Trump fell after his initial attempts to please the president in early 2025. Burnham had the benefit of a fresh start, and ahead of his first meeting with Trump, British officials insisted he would take a less fawning approach than his predecessor. He could afford to do so, they said, because Trump’s presidency is almost at the midway point and there is less to lose. Yet there were similarities to Starmer’s early days. Both leaders were on their best behavior, straining not to upset each other in public. They each gave the other a free pass. Burnham sat expressionless as Trump talked about “fake news” media, while Trump did the same as Burnham talked about Britain’s recent sanctions on West Bank settlements. Burnham raised the salience of immigration, an issue Trump invoked against Starmer, while Trump even praised Burnham’s “great election win.” (Burnham has not won a general election, merely a special election for the parliamentary seat of Makerfield.) But some things were different. The splits between the two nations were closer to the surface than in Starmer’s first trip — and even in those cordial words for the cameras, the divides broke into the open. Advertisement Advertisement Trump seized on a Daily Telegraph journalist’s invitation to condemn the long-stalled British plan to hand sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, a strategically vital archipelago in the Indian Ocean, to Mauritius. His words were little surprise on their own, but Burnham’s response — in which he repeatedly refused to rule out reopening the terms of the deal to satisfy Trump’s concerns — formed a genuine shift in U.K. policy. It remains unclear how any deal could satisfy the demands of Mauritius and the U.S. at the same time. Then there was the gulf between the two leaders on AI regulation. Andy Burnham used his speech to UNGA to put his appeal to domestic cost-of-living issues on a world stage. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Burnham used a breakfast Tuesday in New York with business figures, including Apple’s Tim Cook, to call for an agreed global set of standards on the technology. Barely an hour later, Trump used his speech at the U.N. General Assembly rostrum to condemn “globalist” attempts to regulate what he called “super intelligence.” Burnham spent almost an hour in a room with the leader of the free world (and an eight-strong delegation on each side), yet appears not to have raised AI with Trump at all. Downing Street repeatedly refused to say he brought it up and there was no mention of it the official readout. Advertisement Advertisement After it was all over, Burnham used his speech to UNGA to put his appeal to domestic cost-of-living issues on a world stage. He also announced a “national center for information defense” (with little detail) that would counter disinformation; he portrayed Britain as an “honest broker” on controlling AI. But Britain’s decision not to back a declaration by 22 countries on global AI controls earlier in the week meant it could be sidelined. (Burnham said Britain would look at multiple initiatives, including that one.) There were other potential wrinkles. Burnham said he would speak in defense of the Falkland Islands, weeks after Trump gave fuel to Argentina’s long-standing claims on their sovereignty by suggesting he would not help if Argentina tried to invade. Burnham also revealed that he made a plea to Trump about U.S. tariffs and their effect on a particular factory in the northeast of England (he would not say which one). Despite the carve-outs that Starmer won, British industry — especially the automobile sector — is still being hit by Trump’s tariffs. But so much that could have gone wrong, didn’t — at least for now. Trump did not use the time before the cameras to bring up Britain’s difficult progress toward spending 3.5% of GDP on defense, and did not hit out over the pace of the decision to allow oil and gas drilling in the North Sea. The newbie prime minister looked buttoned-up during the moment for the cameras with Trump, relaxing only when he was asked about Manchester, where he spent nine years as mayor. The world stage is still new to him. Advertisement Advertisement And in that context, his aides will be chalking the first meeting up overall as a win — just as Starmer’s aides did on the way back from New York two years ago this week. Trump praised Burnham as a natural businessman, a man who “gets it.” The vibes, in this relatively easy opening period, were good. He will need to maintain the influence if he can. Burnham later said he lobbied Trump to press for an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia. Pressure on the U.S. to release more air defense missiles to Ukraine ahead of the winter will only increase. While Burnham didn’t invite him to the U.K. on Tuesday, they did pave the way for another visit to one of Trump’s golf resorts. “I said I was having second thoughts about playing golf with him, given a recent performance of my own was probably not up to the right standard,” Burnham told broadcasters. For the man who wasn’t going to bend the knee to Trump, flattery will get him everywhere.

Photograph: Burak Kara/Getty Images Cop31 The planet ‘is being killed’, Greta Thunberg tells Cop31 climate summit Swedish activist criticised world governments for their failure to prevent environmental breakdown Oliver Milman in Antalya Thu 12 Nov 2026 11.39 EST Last modified on Thu 12 Nov 2026 15.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The planet is “not dying, it is being killed and we know by who”, said Greta Thunberg , who excoriated world governments for their failure to prevent environmental breakdown in her first appearance at the annual UN climate talks in five years. Thunberg , 23, the Swedish activist who became famous for heading the school climate strike movement, delivered her stark message to those gathered at the Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, amid the ongoing failure by countries to adequately address the climate crisis. “It [Earth] is being killed by the very same people thought to come to our rescue,” Thunberg said. “No one is coming to our rescue. When our human rights are being threatened by states and other institutions, it’s our duty to stand up and be the adult in the room and fight for everyone’s human rights.” ‘Start listening’: Indigenous activist implores Albanese to block new coal, oil and gas Read more Thunberg, who in recent years has shifted her focus towards other areas such as the conflict in Gaza , linked worsening global heating to other calamities such as war in an appearance alongside activists from Nepal, Canada and Australia. “We are heading towards a future of more genocides and more ecocides and the complete compromise of our basic rights and where basic necessities become luxuries,” she said. “It’s more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be any less under control. The planet is not dying, it is being killed.” The intervention, on the fourth day of the two-week summit, came as world leaders who travelled to the Mediterranean coastal city delivered their own verdicts on the climate crisis and the faltering progress to address it. Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, who was the only G7 leader to attend the talks, said in a speech that the record hot summer in the UK was “not normal”. “The climate crisis is not a distant threat; it is upon us all now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere,” said Burnham, who promised the UK would get to net zero emissions, and backed a proposal for countries to further electrify their economies. View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham, the only G7 leader to attend the talks, said the climate crisis was ‘upon us now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere’. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA Beth John, a climate justice adviser at Oxfam GB, said Burnham’s appearance “sends a positive signal”. But she added: “Showing up is not enough: a crisis of this scale needs substantive action, not just signals. The real test of climate leadership is delivery, not declarations.” The electrification goal is one of the main potential promises expected at the talks, which are being jointly presided over by Turkey and Australia. Some countries want the agreement text to specify that the electricity will be derived from clean energy sources. Campaigners have criticised governments for their slow pace of emissions cuts and for, so far, failing to rally around a phaseout of fossil fuels in the negotiations. Current policies are set to heat the planet by 2.7C by the end of the century, a report by Climate Action Tracker found on Thursday. The catastrophic rise in temperatures is slightly more than the group expected last year and well above the 1.5C that world leaders have promised. View image in fullscreen ‘We call the catastrophic climate change event we suffered a mountain tsunami,’ said Nepal’s environment minister of the flash floods and landslides in the Nuwakot district in August. Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty Images Thursday was rife with accounts of the harm caused by the climate crisis. Gita Chaudhary, Nepal’s environment minister, recounted the disastrous landslide – caused by a melting glacier – that struck the country in August, claiming more than 1,500 lives. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion “We call the catastrophic climate change event we suffered a mountain tsunami,” Chaudhary told the Guardian. “We lost people, we lost lives, we lost property. Nepal is working for rehabilitation, reconstruction and rebuilding the infrastructure. But the communities, the culture, the lives, we cannot revive.” In the main conference room, a speech by Mohammad Mustafa, the prime minister of Palestine, drew a standing ovation from delegates as he described the environmental impact of the three-year war with Israel. “Israel’s restrictions on access to land, water and natural resources have compounded Palestine’s climate challenges,” said Mustafa, who spelled out how widespread destruction in Gaza, including to water supplies, sewerage and farmland, had worsened environmental and health risks. The Turkish hosts of Cop31 have repeatedly accused Israel of genocide and refused to invite the country’s leadership to Antalya. Israel denies that it has committed genocide and insists it has fought a legitimate war to safeguard its own security. View image in fullscreen John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, said Donald Trump was ‘the biggest loser we’ve seen for a long time’ on climate issues. Photograph: Kaan Soyturk/Reuters Another country not formally present at the talks is the US, which did not send a delegation. Donald Trump has withdrawn the country from the international climate framework, derided climate science as a “hoax”, and claimed he would not permit any new wind turbines. This stance earned a rebuke from John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, who has made the trip to Turkey along with 20 Democratic members of Congress and two state governors. “He’s the biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time on all of these issues,” Kerry said of Trump in response to a question from the Guardian. View image in fullscreen Gavin Newsom, the California governor, warned that the Trump administration would ‘double down’ in the remaining presidential term. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters The crushing midterm election win by the Democrats has raised hopes here at Cop of the US re-engaging on the climate crisis. But Gavin Newsom, the governor of California, warned the final two years of the Trump presidency would not see fundamental change on climate policy. “I don’t want to romanticise what this will mean,” Newsom said on Thursday. “I don’t expect they’ll do anything but double down.” Explore more on these topics Cop31 Climate crisis Greta Thunberg Turkey Europe Andy Burnham Extreme weather news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story UK ministers have no plans to publish explosive report on climate crisis Most Europeans want action to tackle climate crisis but not at any cost, poll shows Funding to help poorer countries cope with climate crisis has stalled, says UN National security of all countries at risk due to climate crisis, UK foreign secretary warns ‘Bunch of baloney’: calls grow for Cop summit reforms as countries on track to fail nature targets UN chief urges Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia to turn fossil fuel promises into action US and rest of world must follow China’s lead on green energy, says John Kerry Bottled water and tinned food sales surge after UK government issues emergency stockpile advice High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer’, UN climate chief tells Cop31 Slovenia mourns loss of glacier on its highest peak after scorching summer Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
